absent: Writeback completion, inode cleanup after flush, and migration between dirty, io, and dirty time lists.
Superblock, backing device, and writeback structure lifecycle, registration, and teardown.
Filesystem specific implementations of dirty inode and lazytime synchronization hooks and their journaling effects.
Full permission, mount option, and audit behavior beyond the shown symlink and timestamp checks.
Remaining path walk phases including symlink traversal, final lookup, revalidation, and error recovery.
Definitions of hashing primitives, word loading, rotation, multiplication, and sequence primitives.
Workqueue, timer, and interval configuration beyond delayed wakeup scheduling.
Version query path and change attribute exposure that pairs with the increment barriers.

findings.text: A dirty marking operation first notifies the filesystem so on disk metadata can be updated or journaled, using hooks named dirty_inode and sync_lazytime as alternatives, then records new dirtiness in memory and places first time dirty objects onto a writeback queue with a queueing time, triggering delayed background writeback when needed.

State changes are guarded by a per inode lock named i_lock, with an early lockless check ordered by a barrier against completion. List placement additionally uses a writeback list lock named list_lock, obtained after temporarily releasing the inode lock and then reacquiring it, so flush worker inspection stays atomic. Already queued or special states release locks without insertion.

Flag I_DIRTY_INODE absorbs pending flag I_DIRTY_TIME and clears it from the request, while flag I_DIRTY_PAGES and flag I_DIRTY_TIME are never combined in one request. Objects already carrying any dirty state keep their queue position to preserve time order. States named I_SYNC_QUEUED and I_FREEING prevent list insertion, as does unhashed status except for block devices.

A delayed wakeup helper schedules background writeback after an interval derived from setting dirty_writeback_interval, but only when state WB_registered is present, protecting the decision with a lock named work_lock held with interrupts disabled.

A timestamp update dispatcher routes type FS_UPD_ATIME to an access time path and type FS_UPD_CMTIME to a combined change and modification path, rejecting any other request. The access path is a no operation when current time equals stored access time, otherwise it stores current time and returns a dirtiness indicator.

Timestamp dirtiness depends on mount option SB_LAZYTIME, yielding indicator I_DIRTY_TIME when enabled and indicator I_DIRTY_SYNC otherwise. Combined updates refresh change time unconditionally, refresh modification time only when it differs, and mark dirty only when either timestamp moved. Version handling can upgrade the result to synchronous dirtiness.

Version increment preserves ordering with queries through barriers and an atomic compare exchange loop. The lowest bit holds flag I_VERSION_QUERIED, so increments use step I_VERSION_INCREMENT to skip it. Unforced attempts do nothing unless the queried flag is set, while forced attempts always advance after masking the flag.

When version tracking is enabled, requests with flag IOCB_NOWAIT fail with error EAGAIN without changing timestamps if lazytime is unavailable or a version increment would be required. Blocking lazytime only timestamp updates avoid forcing an increment and let the queried flag decide, preventing unnecessary synchronous dirtiness.

Path initialization moves from flag validation and sequence capture of mount and rename state into one of several start states: preset root, absolute root jump, current working directory, dirfd based start, or scoped start where root is pinned to the start. Read copy update mode records sequence numbers without taking references, while other mode takes references. Relevant markers include LOOKUP_RCU and LOOKUP_IS_SCOPED and ND_JUMPED and ND_ROOT_GRABBED.

Jumping to the real root is forbidden in scoped and beneath constrained walks, and cross device checks forbid leaving the starting mount except for absolute arguments. Missing root state is lazily established. Read copy update handling copies paths and validates sequences, while reference handling exchanges old references for newly pinned root references. Constraints involve LOOKUP_BENEATH and LOOKUP_NO_XDEV and LOOKUP_IS_SCOPED.

Snapshots of process root and current directory use an exclusive read seqlock to copy the path and acquire a reference atomically against concurrent updates, guarded by field seq. Read copy update walkers instead sample with begin and retry loops without taking references, relying on sequence validation.

Link following protection governed by control sysctl_protected_symlinks permits following when follower matches link owner, when the containing directory lacks the combined sticky and world writable mode bits S_ISVTX and S_IWOTH, or when directory owner matches link owner. Read copy update callers request retry on denial, while others emit audit records and deny access.

Nested link depth is counted against limit MAXSYMLINKS, with embedded capacity EMBEDDED_LEVELS handling shallow nesting. Deeper nesting allocates a full table sized to the limit and copies embedded entries. Allocation context depends on walk mode, using atomic allocation for read copy update walks and permitting an unlazy transition with link legitimization before retrying.

Only type LAST_DOTDOT triggers ascent. Resolution clamps at the walk root, otherwise ascends to the parent or, at a mount root, to a suitable mountpoint ancestor that is not above the root. Connectivity is verified for bind mounts. Read copy update failures request retry, while reference mode reports not found or cross device errors. Scoped walks additionally revalidate mount and rename sequences after stepping.

Parent lookup first attempts an optimistic read copy update acquisition with sequence check and conditional reference grab. On failure it locks the candidate parent, revalidates that the parent pointer did not change, and then acquires a stable reference, repeating if a race is detected. Fields involved are d_parent and d_lock and d_seq.

Component hashing folds the parent dentry address with component bytes until slash or terminator, producing a length and hash and a trailing word used for dot detection. One variant processes whole machine words with mixing and final folding, distinguishing single word and multiword components, while the other accumulates byte by byte with incremental and final helpers. One folding uses constant GOLDEN_RATIO_64.

A helper reports that removal may expose a previously hidden mountable ancestor only for normal advancing walks on the same mount without revalidation, when the target is unlinked and flagged as mountable, transferring away the extra reference on success. Exclusions involve WALK_NOFOLLOW and LOOKUP_REVAL.

Distinct failures are signaled by ELOOP for link depth overflow, EXDEV for beneath or cross device violations, ECHILD and EAGAIN for read copy update retry, ENOTRECOVERABLE for scoped root misuse, ENOENT for disconnected parents, EBADF for empty dirfd, ENOMEM for stack exhaustion, ENOTDIR for non directory starts, EACCES for protected link denial, and EIO for unknown timestamp types.

Key state includes inode dirtiness and timing fields named dirtied_when and dirtied_time_when and mode i_mode, superblock hooks, writeback queue membership, and path walk state carrying current and root paths, inode pointer, sequence numbers for dentries mounts and renames, link depth with embedded and overflow stacks, and saved directory mode dir_mode and ownership dir_vfsuid for permission checks.
A path equality helper returns true only when both mount pointer mnt and dentry pointer dentry match, used to detect root confinement and mount root boundaries during traversal.
